Smoke Point in Co-flow Experiment (SPICE)
Abstract
The laminar smoke point is the condition (and the l uminous flame length) where a flame begins
to emit soot. Smoke points indicate the sooting pro pensity of a fuel in diffusion flames. In normal
gravity, laminar smoke points have been measured fo r many gaseous and condensed fuels.
Laminar smoke points have been found to correlate with soot volume fractions and radiative loss
fractions of turbulent diffusion flames. SPICE pro ject measured laminar smoke points in non)
buoyant laminar jet diffusion flames in co)flowing air aboard the International Space Station.
Fifty)two smoke points were found for ethylene, pro pane, propylene, and propylene/nitrogen
mixtures. Burner diameters were 0.41, 0.76, and 1.6 mm and co)flow velocities varied from 5.4 –
65 cm/s. These flames afford extensive control over residence time via variations in dilution,
burner diameter, and co)flow velocity. Increasing c o)flow velocity decreases luminous flame
lengths, but moves smoke points to higher fuel flow rates and longer luminous flame lengths.
Smaller burners have longer smoke points for co)flo wing flames. These trends can be explained
qualitatively by considering total residence time e ffects. The luminous flame lengths generally
correlate with fuel mass flow rate divided by stoic hiometric mixture fraction, although they
increase slightly as air velocity decreases. The me asured smoke point lengths were found to
correlate with burner diameter to the –0.91 power t imes coflow velocity to the 0.41 power. The
measurements allow estimates of pseudo threshold so ot indices (TSI) for microgravity diffusion
flames, indicating an unusually high sooting propen sity for propane in microgravity. A model of
residence times in coflowing flames is developed, a nd although residence time helps explain
many of the observations, it does not correlate the measured smoke points. The measurements
yielded estimates of sooting propensities of the present fuels in microgravity diffusion flames.

INTRODUCTION

SPICE project, from it was rewarded in 1997 to it w as conducted onboard ISS in 2009, covered
more than a decade time span. During these years, t he project experienced a few cycles of active and
inactive status. A brief project history is given b elow. SPICE project was awarded on December 3,
1997 by the Microgravity Science and Application Di vision of NASA Headquarters to Professor
Gerard M. Faeth of the University of Michigan for h is proposal titled as Laminar Smoke Point
Properties of Nonbuoyant Round-Jet Diffusion Flames in response to NASA’s 1996 Solicitation for
Glovebox Investigations issued in late 1996. The or iginal proposal of Professor Faeth was meant to
be a supplement to the Laminar Soot Processes Exper iment which was a combustion project under
NASA Grant No. NAG3-1245, conducted onboard STS-73 and STS-94 in 1997. In the awarding
letter, the experiment was planned to be carried out onboard STS-107, for which the launch date was
then scheduled in May 2000. From December 1997 to t he end of 1999 was the first phase of the
project. In this period, the experiment was planned to be conducted in the Middle Deck Glove Box
of a Space Shuttle and the SPICE hardware was fabri cated and assembled in GRC. Various project
reviews necessary for the flight project, were comp leted. In addition, significant efforts on science
side were made to explore proper camera settings fo r different flame conditions by conducting
reduced gravity experiment in parabolic flight on board the KC-135 aircraft. From the end of 1999 to
March 2002, the project was inactive. The second p hase of the project was from March 2002 to
January 2005. In this period, SPICE was a part of MRDOC contract to ZIN Inc., for a potential UF-1
Flight. Since the target facility of SPICE was swit ched from Space Shuttle’s Middle Deck Glove
Box to the ISS Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG), ZIN’s major effort was to retro-fit hardware
for use with MSG in International Space Station (IS S), which included: designed and assembled
Power/Video Unit to support MSG video interfaces, d esigned and fabricated a new mechanical
camera supports, redesigned fuel bottle assemblies and developed new cabling. Project was
cancelled again at the end of 2004. ZIN developed s torage plan for hardware which was presented to
NASA in December, 2004. The SPICE apparatus was put in storage in January 2005 and all the
documents were archived waiting for future flight o pportunities. At that time, the LSP project and
the re-flight LSP-2 were completed, thus the object ives of SPICE were later changed to a stand-
alone investigation of smoke point of jet diffusion flames with coexistence of air flows.

matrix was finalized. Additional tests in camera were conducted.

Minor hardware modifications were made and a number of project reviews were conducted. The
SPICE hardware was shipped to KSC on June 18, 2008 and later lifted up to ISS by ULF-2 in
October 2008. SPICE experiments were finally conduc ted in ISS MSG from February through June
of 2009. What Follows is the science significance and justification of the SPICE project.

Soot formation in hydrocarbon-fueled flames is an i mportant unresolved problem in combustion
science. Soot is estimated to be responsible for up to 52,000 premature deaths annually in the U.S. 1
and is believed to contribute to climate change and glacial melting. 2 Radiation from soot in flames is
beneficial in many applications but also contributes to unwanted heat loads in engines and the spread
of fires. Carbon monoxide emitted by smoking flames is the major cause of death in fires. 3
Knowledge of Soot formation is needed for developing computational combustion.

2

The differences between soot processes in buoyant a nd nonbuoyant laminar jet diffusion flames can
be seen by comparing their soot production regions as plotted in Fig. 1. Soot formation in diffusion
flames generally is limited to fuel-equivalence rat ios, φ, in the range 1-2, which are marked on the
plots. Unlike gases, which both convect and diffus e, soot mainly convects with the flow velocity so
that it moves along the streamline. For buoyant fl ames, the dividing streamline generally is inside
the soot formation region so that most of the soot initially forms near the flame sheet, where φ, =1,
and then moves radially inward toward cooler region s having higher fuel concentrations. The soot
formation process for nonbuoyant flames is complete ly different: most of the soot initially forms
near the cool core of the flame, where φ is close to 2, and is drawn directly toward the fl ame sheet.
Results from an MSL-1 combustion project, the Lamin ar Soot Processes (LSP), revealed that the
smoke height phenomenon in microgravity can be subs tantially different form that seen in normal
gravity. The removal of buoyancy induced accelerat ion can cause the smoke point phenomenon to
be dominated by radiative heat losses for condition s of low overall flame velocity. Under these
conditions the flame extinguishes at the flame tip allowing soot to be emitted. In spite of this effe ct,
it is still possible to have flames that either emi t soot along all stream lines or do not emit soot
anywhere, for conditions where radiation losses do not dominate.

Figure 1. Soot path lines through buoyant and non-b uoyant flames

The information of smoke-point properties and flame shapes is needed to improve our understanding
of heat and mass transfer mechanisms for different flame conditions. Unfortunately, while the
laminar smoke-point properties of buoyant jet diffu sion flames at normal gravity are well known,
corresponding information for nonbuoyant flames is limited and questionable. Thus the insights of
soot generation and oxidation processes under micro gravity conditions are critical to devise better
fire safety strategy in spacecraft needed for long term space travels and other space exploration
activities. In addition, the improved understanding of soot processes in laminar flames will help us,
by analogy, to gain better understanding of soot processes in practical turbulent flames.

The objectives of the SPICE experiments is to find the laminar smoke-point properties of non-
buoyant jet diffusion flames for several fuels unde r different nozzle diameter/co-flow velocity
configurations. Luminous flame shape measurements would also be made to verify models of the

3

flame shapes under co-flow conditions. In particula r, the experiments are planned to be conducted
under the following conditions: six types of fuels: methane, ethylene, propane, propylene, 75%
propylene mixed with 25% nitrogen in moles, and 50% propylene mixed with 50% nitrogen in moles;
three nozzles: 0.4, 0.8 and 1.6 mm ID and two air v elocities: 100% and 50% of the maximum air
flow velocity (near 50cm/s). The operation procedur es are as such that the air velocity is set first,
then start the fuel flow and ignite the flame. Fuel flow rate is adjusted until the smoke point is
reached. Thus, for each combination of a fuel and a nozzle size, two smoke point fuel flow rates are
obtained. One is under 100% air velocity and the ot her is under 50% air velocity. Then in the case of
50% air velocity, the fuel flow rate is reduced to 50% of the smoke point fuel flow rate to get a flame
length with that fuel flow rate.

SPICE EXPERIMENT SETUP
A. The SPICE Apparatus
The SPICE project utilized and modified an apparatu s constructed for a previous project, Enclosed
Laminar Flames (ELF), which was conducted in the Mi ddle Deck Glovebox of Space Shuttle
Columbia during mission USMP-4/STS-87 in November, 1997. The SPICE apparatus configuration
and the connection to the MSG power supply are show n in Figure 2. The upper right portion in the
figure, separated by dashed lines includes the part s placed inside the Glovebox, whereas the rest
parts are outside the Glovebox, either for astronauts to control or monitor the experiment inside.

Figure 2. Schematic of SPICE experiment apparatus a nd its connection with SMG. The
upper-right portion separated by dash lines are the SPICE apparatus.

4

Inside the Glovebox, the core of the apparatus is t he Experimental Assembly which consists of a
flow duct and its accessories. In this flow duct bu rns the flame under investigation. More detailed
discuss of this part will be given below. An imagi ng system, including a still digital camera and a
video camera is mounted outside the flow duct to re cord the flame images. Inside the Glovbox there
are two additional enclosures. One is the Power Uni t that converts the electrical power provided by
the Glovebox Power Supply (single voltage) to vario us voltages needed by different part of the
SPICE apparatus. The second enclosure is the Video Unit which has the following functions: a)
controls the shutter of the still cameras based on the signal received from the control box, and b)
merges the video camera signal with the signal from a title generator which includes air and fuel
flow rates and outputs the merged signal to a VCR o utside the Glovebox for recording and
displaying on a monitor. The feature of merging fla me image and the flow rates to a single video
image is very important improvement of SPICE over E LF. With the real time flow rates stamped on
the flame image, the data reduction process, after the experiment, is greatly simplified by eliminating
the need of synchronizing the flame image and the f low data manually, which would be very tedious
and time consuming.

As shown in Fig. 2, outside the Glovebox there are two parts: a control box that astronauts hold to
control the experiment in the flow duct and a video recording and display part for astronauts to
watch the flame during burn, because astronauts need to determine when the flame starts to emit soot
and when a still image should be taken. More detailed discussion of each part is given below.

Experiment Assembly: Figure 3 shows a photo of the Experiment Assembly.

The flow duct is the core of the Assembly. The inte rior dimensions of the flow duct are 172mm x
43mm x 43mm. It has two Lexan windows on its top an d front sides through which the still camera
and the video camera can image the flame.

A retractable ruler 105mm in length is placed insid e the flow duct. It is used to generate a reference
image for flame length measurement. This ruler is n ormally rests at the far, bottom corner of the
flow duct. When a reference image is taken, it is m oved in line with the nozzle tip. Since its surface
is 45 degree tilted, it can be seen both by the sti ll camera and the video camera. After the reference

image is taken, the ruler is moved back to its home position. The ruler is mechanically linked to and
controlled by a handle outside of the flow duct, at its front right corner.

A hot wire igniter, a coiled Kanthal wire, was used to ignite the flame. During ignition, it is moved
to the nozzle tip through a handle next to the rule r handle and electrically powered up with about 4
amps of electric current that makes the wire bright red hot. Once the flame ignition is confirmed, the
igniter is then moved away from the nozzle tip to i ts home position. The two handles are designed in
such that only one of the two, the igniter and the ruler, can be moved to the nozzle at a certain time .
This provides a safety feature of the system that p revents the ruler from being burned by the igniter.
There is a small magnet mounted on the linkage to t he igniter and a Hall-effect sensor mounted on
the hinge of the front door. This sensor controls t he igniter power circuits that when the front door is
in open position or when the igniter is at its home position, the igniter power circuit is disabled. I n
other words, the igniter can be powered only if the front door is closed and the igniter is at the nozzle
tip. The igniter is replaceable. When replacing the igniter, the astronaut must open the front door so
that the igniter will not be powered during the replacement.

There are 3 fuel nozzles made for the SPICE experim ent. They all have the same length; 50 mm,
with different inner diameters: 0.41 mm, 0.76 mm an d 1.6 mm, respectively. Only one of the three
nozzles is installed during a burn. Figure 4 is a p hoto of the igniters and nozzles in a storage box
shipped to ISS. It can be seen that a nozzle has tw o parts: a thicker base with female threads in it and
a piece of thin tubing extended from the base. Thu s the nozzle is threaded on a connector inside the
flow duct, on the left hand side in Fig. 3. After installation, the nozzle is along the center line of flow
duct. Its tip is about 54 mm from the screen at the left end of the flow duct.

A thermopile radiometer, Oriel Model 71768, is plac ed in the far right corner downstream of the
duct. It has a 90 degree view angle that can bracke t the entire flame length. Since the radiometer
signal is an integrated result of flame radiation, which is a complicated function of flame shape and
temperature distribution in the flame, it can only provide a qualitative measurement of flame
radiation. The flame radiation varies in a wide ran ge depending on flame conditions so that the
radiometer amplifier is equipped with a gain contro l switch to ensure the signal is detected with
proper accuracy.

1179A52CS1BV-S, 0 - 500 SCCM, Standard Conditions: 0 oC and 760 Torr), and stainless steel

The module is also equipped with data logger and PCMCIA storage.

B. Air velocity distribution in the flow duct
An important feature of SPICE is that it has air co -flow surrounding the flames. SPICE is the first
experiment that studies soot processes of laminar j et diffusion flame under long term microgravity
condition with air coflow. Because the velocity dis tribution in or near the flame is complicated by
the varying gas property and thermal expansion, the coflow air velocity can only be specified in far
field and the inlet of the flow duct as boundary co nditions of the flame under investigation. For this
reason, the information of air velocity distributio n before igniting of the flame is needed. The air
velocity was measured with an anemometer at differe nt locations in the flow duct at different fan
speed. The top window and the front window were rep laced by two windows with holes on them to
accommodate anemometer prob. Figure 13 shows vario us hole locations through which air
velocities were measured. Some expressions used in describing a spatial location are explained as
follows. A “Station” refers to a plane perpendicula r to the flow direction. The value of a “Station”
indicates the distance between the nozzle tip and t he plane. There are only two Stations in use: 13
mm and 56 mm, defining two planes 13 mm and 56 mm d ownstream of the nozzle tip. “Height Off
Floor” refers to the distance above the floor of th e flow duct. The Floor of the flow duct is the lowe r
wall of the flow duct, perpendicular to the front w indow. The three positions in Height Off Floor in
use are 19 mm, 36 mm, and 57 mm define three planes in parallel with the flow duct floor. The 36
mm one is in the middle of the flow duct so that it includes the nozzle. The third direction is
expressed in terms of “Centerline”, “20 mm to the Inside” and “20 mm to the Outside,” which define
three planes in parallel with the front window of t he flow duct. There are totally 18 intersections of
these three sets of planes. Air velocities were mea sured at these 18 locations at 6 different fan dial
settings.

The third direction is
expressed in terms of “Centerline”, “20 mm to the Inside” and “20 mm to the Outside,” which define
three planes in parallel with the front window of t he flow duct. There are totally 18 intersections of
these three sets of planes. Air velocities were mea sured at these 18 locations at 6 different fan dial
settings. Note that for the safety concern, even at 0 fan dial setting, there is a minimum DC voltage
applied to the fan to maintain a low velocity air f low which prevents fuel gas from accumulating in
the flow duct.

SPICE FLIGHT TESTS
The actual SPICE tests were conducted in SMG in twelve sessions from February 14, 2009 to June
23, 2009. In each session, the SPICE science team and engineering team were in the TeleScience
Center (TSC) in GRC to support the tests conducted on MSG. Real-time flame images were
available as long as air-to-ground communication channel was available. In addition, the team was
able to communicate with the astronaut who conducted the experiment to answer questions or to
clarify any ambiguities.

Most tests were conducted by setting the coflow vel ocity, igniting the flame, and adjusting the fuel
flow rate. Approximate smoke points were identified in the video by the flight crew and
simultaneously by the ground support team in TSC. Typical burn times were 60 s, and after each two
such burns the MSG contents were flushed with ISS c abin air. The oxygen mole fraction of this
cabin air is maintained within 19 – 24%.

After the tests the video record was analyzed to id entify smoke points. The smoke point lengths, LSP ,
(and the flow conditions) were obtained from the vi deo record and are the measured distance from
the burner to the tip of the luminous flame on the flame axis. The luminous flame tips were not
sharply defined in most images, but rather transiti oned from bright yellow to black over an axial
distance of 2 – 5 mm. Luminous lengths were measure d to the point where the centerline grayscale

Totally 526 flames were ignited and studied, which were much more than originally planned. The

The flames generally reached steady conditions within 5 s of ignition or a change in flow rate of fuel

attributed to increased soot volume fractions. Peri odic flame motion was observed in some flames,
especially those with high air velocity, large burn ers, and long flames, and is attributed to coflow
perturbations. This increased slightly the uncertainties in smoke points for these conditions.

TEST RESULTS
Smoke points were attempted for all fuels. The cond itions for which smoke points were found are
summarized in Table 1. In some cases (e.g., tests i nvolving ethylene) the fuel supply was depleted
before all desired conditions could be tested, as t he supply was limited to two 150 cc bottles of each
fuel at gage pressures of 760 – 1440 kPa. Smoke poi nts were attempted with methane, but could not
be obtained before the flames impinged on the copper plate at the end of the duct.

Some smoke points (particularly for propane and eth ylene) were identified by the onset of gradual
dimming, reddening, and rounding of the luminous fl ame tip. Conversely, the brightest flames
(particularly for propylene and propylene mixtures) normally did not display significant dimming
and reddening near their tips, except when much lon ger than their smoke points. For these flames,
smoke points were identified by the rapid transitio n to open-tipped flames. Open-tipped flames are
common in microgravity when smoke points are far ex ceeded 4 and are associated with flame
extinguishment along the centerline and soot that e scapes in an annular shell. For conditions
sufficiently above the smoke points, quenched soot could be seen leaving the flames despite the dark
background in the video.

Figure 17 shows images for representative flames ne ar their smoke points. Two sequences are
shown, and in both, the smoke point occurs between the third and fourth images. In the top row,
coflow velocity decreases from left to right at a c onstant fuel flow rate. This increases luminous
flame length and leads to soot emission in the four th image. The luminous length decreases in the
fourth image owing to flame extinction and extensiv e reactant leakage. In the bottom row, fuel flow
rate is increased at a constant coflow velocity, in creasing luminous lengths. The luminous lengths of
the flames in Fig. 17 are more sensitive to changes in fuel flow rate than to changes in coflow
velocity. For a jet diffusion flame, the fuel flow rate is the limiting factor of the flame length because
there is almost unlimited amount of oxidant (air in this case) available. This is why the flame length
is more sensitive to the change of fuel flow rate.

In Fig. 18 the measured smoke point lengths are plo tted with respect to coflow velocity. For a given
choice of fuel and burner diameter, an increase in coflow velocity generally increases the smoke
point length. This behavior is attributed to decrea sed residence times and radiative losses as coflow
velocity increases, and is an important issue for f urther consideration. The slope of the correlations
in Fig. 18 generally decreases with increased sooting propensity. Figure 18 reveals that smoke points
of nonbuoyant coflowing flames decrease with increasing burner diameter. This behavior also can be
attributed to effects of residence time, as fuel velocity is proportional to d–2 when fuel mass flow rate
is constant.

DISCUSSION

Although it is convenient to classified all flames, laminar vs. turbulent and diffusion vs. premixed,
into two categories based on their soot emission co nditions, i.e., soot emitting flames and non-soot
emitting flames, the conditions delineating the two or the conditions of onset of soot emission are
difficult to define. Up to date, these conditions h ave been documented solely based on experimental
observations. Many efforts have been made to dev elop a universal method of defining the onset of
soot emission, i.e., smoke point, conditions, in terms of primary parameters of the flame. But none of
these efforts has been quite successful yet. The primary parameters of the flame mentioned here refer
to parameters used to set the flame, not those gene rated by the flame. The primary parameters of jet
diffusion flames include fuel type, fuel and oxidiz er supply rates, ambient temperature and pressure,
and configuration of the device where the flame takes place, such as nozzle diameter and dimensions
of the combustion chamber. The flame temperature, g as velocity and species distributions as well as
flame shapes and derived parameters such as heat ge neration and heat loss, are the parameters
generated by the flame which is not considered as p rimary parameters. If a method that relates
smoke point to those primary parameters were found, we would be able to predict whether a flame
emits soot or not based on the planned flame condit ions. In the course of pursuing such a universal
method, a number of surmises of the mechanism of so ot emission have been proposed to associate
smoke point with certain flame generated parameters . Those surmises served as a middle step in
hoping to help further development of the aforement ioned method. The first surmise, and least
controversial, is that smoke points occur when soot temperature drops below a critical temperature
prior to soot burnout. This temperature is about 13 00 K in normal gravity 8,9 and 1000 K in
microgravity.10,11 The second is that smoke point occurs when radiati ve loss fraction reaches 0.2 –
0.4 for normal-gravity flames 12-16 or 0.4 – 0.6 for microgravity flames. 17 Since the radiative fraction
of heat loss increases with fuel flow rate, smoke p oint will occur as the fuel flow rate is higher tha n

certain value. This is consistent with experimental observations. The third surmise is that the smoke
point correlates to the ratio of luminous length di vided by stoichiometric length. This ratio increase s
with flow rate. Once it reaches about 2, smoke poin t occurs. 15,18,19 The last surmise suggests that
smoke point correlates with the centerline flame re sidence time. This is the most complex 8-11,17,18,20-
24 surmise because flame residence time affects the s oot processes in twofold. An increase in
residence time can lead to soot emissions by increa sing the time available for soot formation.
Because this generally also increases the time avai lable for soot oxidation, it has been proposed that
smoke points are associated with conditions where t he time available for soot formation exceeds that
for soot oxidation to certain extent. 21 This is difficult to prove because to evaluate the flame
residence time requires the velocity distribution a lone the centerline and the flame length, both of
which are resulted flame parameters, not readily av ailable from primary parameters of the
experiment. In addition, the soot formation time an d oxidation time are conceptually defined.
Practically, these times are not measurable and the y might be overlapped, i.e., for the same soot
aggregate, adding and oxidizing carbon particles ma y happen simultaneously. Because of these
difficulties and ambiguities, the fame residence ti me theory cannot be proved or disproved
rigorously. However, these obstacles do not preven t us from checking the residence time theory
against the observed smoke point data with the help of some approximated velocity distribution and
flame length information. More detailed discussion of this effort can be found in the publications
resulted from the SPICE project listed in Appendice s B through F. The results showed that although
residence time is helpful in understanding the pres ent smoke points, it does not yield quantitative
correlations.

CLOSING REMARKS
Smoke points of 55 microgravity gas-jet diffusion f lames in coflowing air were measured in earth
orbit. The conditions emphasized small burners and the effects of coflow velocity. These flames
allow extensive control over residence time, which is important in smoke point phenomena. The
major conclusions are as follows:
1. An increase in coflow velocity increases the smoke point length.
2. A decrease in burner diameter increases the smoke point length.
3. These two effects can be explained qualitatively by considering residence times; increased
fuel and/or coflow velocities yield increased smoke point lengths.
